title: std::vector Iterator Invalidation During Erase in Loop
symptoms: Crash with segfault or skipped elements when erasing items inside a standard vector iteration loop.
roast: Erasing the track beneath your minecart while still rolling on it: high speed derailment guaranteed.
diagnosis: Calling vec.erase(it) invalidates the erased iterator and all subsequent iterators in std::vector. Continuing to increment an invalidated iterator causes undefined behavior.
debuggingSteps: Assign the iterator to the return value of erase(): it = vec.erase(it)
Alternatively, use the modern C++20 std::erase_if algorithm
Do not unconditionally increment '++it' when an element is removed
whyItWorks: vec.erase(it) returns an iterator following the removed element, maintaining a valid traversal cursor without skipping or reading invalid memory.
tests: std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3}; for(auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end();) { if(*it == 2) it = v.erase(it); else ++it; } assert(v.size() == 2 && v[1] == 3);

title: Object Slicing When Passing Polymorphic Classes by Value
symptoms: Derived class member variables and overridden virtual methods are ignored or lost when passed to a function.
roast: Crafting a diamond sword, but dropping it into a wooden sword slot: you just sliced off the diamond blade.
diagnosis: Passing polymorphic types by value invokes the base copy constructor, constructing only the base subobject and discarding (slicing) the derived portion.
debuggingSteps: Check function signature taking polymorphic Base parameter by value
Change parameter to pass by reference (const Base&) or pointer (std::unique_ptr<Base>)
Verify virtual dispatch resolves to Derived implementation
whyItWorks: Passing by reference retains the full derived dynamic type in memory and enables virtual method dispatch through the vtable.
tests: Derived d; const Base &b = d; assert(b.getName() == "Derived");

title: Missing Virtual Destructor in Base Class
symptoms: Derived class destructors are never invoked when deleting through base pointer, leaking member resources.
roast: Destroying a chest with an axe, but only deleting the lid while all the diamonds remain orphaned in limbo.
diagnosis: Deleting an object through a pointer to Base when Base does not declare a virtual destructor results in undefined behavior (C++ Standard [expr.delete]) and skips Derived cleanup.
debuggingSteps: Locate base classes with virtual methods
Declare 'virtual ~Base() = default;' in the base class definition
Run AddressSanitizer or leak sanitizer to confirm complete cleanup
whyItWorks: A virtual destructor ensures the runtime uses vtable dispatch to execute Derived's destructor before tearing down Base.
tests: Base *b = new Derived(); delete b; // Derived destructor executed without leaks

title: Cyclic Memory Leak via Circular std::shared_ptr
symptoms: Objects managed by std::shared_ptr never get destroyed, leaking memory indefinitely despite falling out of scope.
roast: Two Redstone repeaters pointing into each other: infinite loop, zero progress, perpetual lockup.
diagnosis: When object A holds a shared_ptr to B and B holds a shared_ptr to A, their reference counts never drop to zero, preventing deallocation.
debuggingSteps: Identify back-references or parent-child pointer relationships
Break ownership cycles by converting non-owning back-references to std::weak_ptr
Inspect use_count() during debugging to detect stuck counts
whyItWorks: std::weak_ptr observes the managed object without incrementing the strong reference counter, allowing destructors to trigger naturally when strong owners release.
tests: auto n1 = std::make_shared<Node>(); auto n2 = std::make_shared<Node>(); n1->next = n2; n2->prev = n1; assert(n1.use_count() == 1);

title: Dangling std::string_view from Temporary std::string
symptoms: Garbage characters, memory corruption, or intermittent segfaults when inspecting string_view data.
roast: Peeking through a spyglass at a sunset that already turned to midnight: you are viewing dead pixels.
diagnosis: std::string_view does not own underlying string storage. Binding a string_view to a temporary std::string leaves it dangling once the temporary statement ends.
debuggingSteps: Check functions returning string_view referencing local string concatenations
Return std::string by value if the function generates a new string
Ensure the backing string outlives any string_view referencing it
whyItWorks: Returning std::string by value transfers ownership of the underlying buffer to the caller instead of leaving an unowned view into dead stack space.

title: Accessing Moved-From Object (Use-After-Move)
symptoms: Empty containers, null pointers, or invalid state after passing an object with std::move.
roast: You moved all your iron into the chest and then tried to craft armor from your empty inventory.
diagnosis: std::move casts an lvalue to an rvalue, allowing ownership to be pilfered. The moved-from object is left in a valid but unspecified state, typically hollowed out.
debuggingSteps: Audit code using an object after passing it into std::move
Re-initialize or assign the object before subsequent reads
Pass const reference if caller still requires read access
whyItWorks: Copying preserves the source vector's elements, ensuring src retains valid elements for subsequent indexing.
tests: std::vector<int> src = {1, 2, 3}; auto dest = src; assert(src.size() == 3 && dest.size() == 3);

title: Dangling Reference in Lambda Capture [&]
symptoms: Intermittent corruption or segfault when asynchronous callbacks or stored lambdas are executed.
roast: Storing a map with tether lines tied to sand blocks: the moment sand drops, your lines snap.
diagnosis: Capturing automatic variables by reference ([&] or [&var]) inside a lambda that outlives the enclosing function scope leaves dangling references to popped stack frames.
debuggingSteps: Inspect lambdas returned from functions or dispatched across threads
Switch from reference capture [&] to value capture [=] or explicit init capture [val = var]
Use std::shared_ptr if shared state is needed across asynchronous tasks
whyItWorks: Capturing factor by value copies the integer into the lambda closure object, ensuring its lifetime is bound to the lambda itself.

title: Dangling Member Reference to Temporary in Constructor
symptoms: Member references contain corrupted data when accessed outside constructor body.
roast: Binding your leash to a ghost: as soon as the constructor finishes, your horse runs wild.
diagnosis: While binding a temporary to a local const reference extends its lifetime, binding a temporary to a class reference member does NOT extend its lifetime past constructor execution.
debuggingSteps: Avoid storing raw reference members (const T&) inside classes unless lifetime is strictly managed
Store member variables by value or smart pointer
Verify constructor parameters outlive the constructed class instance
whyItWorks: Storing the string by value inside Holder ensures the string data is owned by and tied to the lifetime of the Holder instance.

title: Pointer Invalidation Caused by std::vector Reallocation
symptoms: Reading through an element pointer or reference yields stale or garbage data after calling push_back.
roast: Renovating your castle by bulldozing the foundation while your buddy is still standing on the 2nd floor.
diagnosis: When std::vector exceeds its current capacity, push_back allocates a new larger buffer, copies elements over, and frees old memory, invalidating all existing pointers.
debuggingSteps: Call vec.reserve(N) ahead of time if pointers/references to elements are cached
Store indices rather than pointers or references to vector elements
Avoid caching pointers across push_back or emplace_back calls
whyItWorks: Reserving capacity guarantees no heap reallocation takes place during subsequent push_backs within the reserved limit.
tests: std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(5); v.push_back(10); int *p = &v[0]; v.push_back(20); assert(*p == 10);

title: Exception Thrown in Destructor Triggers std::terminate
symptoms: Process abruptly terminates with 'terminate called after throwing an instance of...' without catching exception.
roast: Blowing up a TNT block inside your base while cleaning up spider webs: instant rage quit.
diagnosis: Since C++11, destructors are noexcept(true) by default. Throwing an exception from a destructor (especially during stack unwinding) immediately invokes std::terminate.
debuggingSteps: Audit destructors to guarantee no unhandled exceptions can escape
Enclose potentially throwing calls inside try-catch blocks within the destructor
Log errors rather than throwing exceptions during destruction cleanup
whyItWorks: Catching all internal exceptions inside the destructor prevents exceptions from escaping, preserving the noexcept contract and preventing std::terminate.
tests: { Resource r; } // Exits scope smoothly without throwing or terminating
